title: Decorator pattern
idea: The Decorator pattern wraps an object in another object with the same interface, adding behaviour before or after each forwarded call, without editing the original class.

analogy.text: A phone in a rugged case, then a card wallet clipped on. Each layer adds one feature, and you still use the phone the same way.
analogy.breaks: A case cannot change what the phone does; a decorator can change results.

points: A decorator implements the component interface and wraps one instance of it.
Each method adds its step and forwards the call; wrapping order sets step order.
`java.io` uses it: a `BufferedReader` wraps a `FileReader` to add buffering.
Use it for optional, combinable extras; one fixed extra step needs no pattern.

steps.caption: The caller holds a `PaymentGateway`. It cannot tell how many wrappers sit behind it.
`Logging` adds its before-step, then forwards to the object it wraps.
`LimitCheck` sees 2500 is under the limit, so it forwards too.
`Retrying` makes attempt 1 on the real gateway.
`CardGateway` times out and throws. Only `Retrying` is built to handle that.
`Retrying` catches the exception and calls the gateway again. This time it pays.
The result unwinds through each wrapper. `Logging` adds its after-step on the way out.
A 50000 charge stops at `LimitCheck`. The inner layers never run.

code.title: The problem: subclasses
code.caption: Adding features by inheritance: every mix needs its own class, and code gets copied.

walk.text: Four classes already, for only two features on one gateway.
Logging is welded to `CardGateway`. A wallet gateway needs its own copy.
The limit check is welded to the card gateway too.
This copies the logging lines. It logs, then `super.charge` checks the limit: order fixed at compile time.
Add retry as a third feature: each gateway needs 7 subclasses (2^3 - 1), so two need 14.

code.title: The fix: decorators
code.caption: Three small wrappers, each with one job, stacked around any `PaymentGateway`.

walk.text: The component interface. Callers and every wrapper depend only on this.
The concrete component does the real work. It fails once to trigger retry.
The base decorator holds the wrapped object. `requireNonNull` rejects a missing one early.
`Logging` acts before and after forwarding, and returns the inner result unchanged.
`LimitCheck` may short-circuit: an over-limit charge never reaches the inner layers.
`Retrying` calls the inner object again on failure, then rethrows after the last attempt.
Composition happens at runtime. Reorder the constructors to change the behaviour.

pitfalls: Putting `LimitCheck` inside `Retrying` re-checks the limit on every attempt; decide the wrapping order on purpose.
Code that checks `instanceof CardGateway` breaks once the object is wrapped; depend on the interface.
A `default` interface method a decorator forgets to override silently skips the wrapped object.

quiz.q: Same classes as the demo. How many times does `log: charge B-7` print?
quiz.why: `Logging` is inside `Retrying`, so each attempt passes through it. The first attempt times out, the second pays: two before-steps.

takeaway: A decorator is the same interface plus one extra step, wrapped around another.
